<section class="page-hero"><h1>Princeton University</h1><p class="lead">Princeton, New Jersey · United States · June 2023</p></section>
<main class="content"><div class="content-inner fieldwork-story princeton-story">

<figure class="fieldwork-hero"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-10.webp" alt="Participants in the Ritual and Materiality in Buddhism and Asian Religions conference at Princeton" loading="eager"><figcaption>A research stay at Princeton centered on an international conference devoted to the relationship between ritual and materiality in Asian religions.</figcaption></figure>

<p class="lead">I had the honor of being selected to take part in <a href="https://ritualmateriality2023.princeton.edu/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><em>Ritual and Materiality in Buddhism and Asian Religions</em></a>, an international conference held at Princeton University in June 2023. During a week in Princeton, whose scholarly core was the June 13–15 conference, I joined a group of only twenty doctoral students from around the world. Nearly ninety graduate applications had been considered; selection was based on the quality of the research and its relevance to the conference themes. My dissertation project on the evolution of Buddhist court art in Korea and its patrons was listed among the selected research topics.</p>

<h2>Princeton and the history of American higher education</h2>
<p>Arriving at Princeton also meant entering one of the oldest institutional landscapes in American higher education. Founded in 1746 as the <em>College of New Jersey</em>, it was the fourth college established in British North America. The college moved to Princeton and Nassau Hall in 1756, officially became Princeton University in 1896, and established its Graduate School at the turn of the twentieth century. Nassau Hall even served as the meeting place of the Continental Congress in 1783. That history gave a particular resonance to a conference positioned at the intersection of Buddhist studies, art history, East Asian studies, and the study of religion. <a href="https://profile.princeton.edu/about-princeton-university" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read Princeton’s institutional history.</a></p>

<div class="figure-pair"><figure class="figure-item"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-01.webp" alt="Architecture on the Princeton University campus" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The historic campus formed the everyday setting for research and conversation.</figcaption></figure><figure class="figure-item"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-08.webp" alt="Princeton University building" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Moving between sessions made the institution’s historical depth physically tangible.</figcaption></figure></div>

<h2>Ritual, objects, and bodies</h2>
<p>The conference asked what changes when Buddhism and Asian religions are studied not only through doctrines and texts, but through manuscripts, paintings, images, statues, talismans, ritual implements, technologies, and bodily engagement. That connection between practice, image, and materiality was especially close to my own work as an art historian.</p>

<div class="figure-pair"><figure class="figure-item"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-02.webp" alt="Conference session on Amitabha devotion" loading="lazy"><figcaption>A session in which images, inscriptions, and devotional practices were analyzed together.</figcaption></figure><figure class="figure-item"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-03.webp" alt="Presentation of Buddhist ritual objects" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Ritual objects were treated as active components of religious practice, not merely as illustrations.</figcaption></figure></div>

<p>The format mattered as much as the topic. Twenty-one scholars from Asia, Europe, and North America joined the panels, while the twenty selected PhD students were incorporated into the discussion. Papers were circulated beforehand, allowing the sessions to focus on critical exchange rather than a sequence of read presentations. Art history, religious history, anthropology, textual studies, archaeology, and ritual studies therefore met in a genuinely comparative setting.</p>

<h2>Shu-fen Liu’s keynote</h2>
<figure class="fieldwork-figure-wide"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-04.webp" alt="Screen for the keynote on Arhat cave worship" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The keynote examined Arhat cave worship and the Daitokuji paintings of the Five Hundred Arhats.</figcaption></figure>

<p>The keynote was delivered by <strong>Shu-fen Liu (劉淑芬)</strong> of the Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica. A historian of medieval China and the social history of Buddhism from the third to the thirteenth century, she has worked extensively on ritual practices, inscriptions, and Arhat worship. Her lecture, <em>The Arhat Cave Belief in Four Stele Inscriptions and the Daitokuji Paintings of Five Hundred Arhats</em>, brought cave inscriptions, cultic topography, and painting cycles into a single argument. For me, it was a compelling demonstration of how material art history can connect texts, spaces, images, and ritual action.</p>

<h2>An interdisciplinary group of scholars</h2>
<p>The two main discussants embodied the conference’s methodological range. <strong>Laurel Kendall</strong>, curator of Asian ethnographic collections at the American Museum of Natural History, is known for anthropological work on Korean shamanism and the ritual life of images and objects in Korea and Southeast Asia. <strong>Justin McDaniel</strong>, professor at the University of Pennsylvania, works on Southeast Asian Buddhism, Pali and Sanskrit, manuscripts, architecture, and religious practice. Their presence made clear that materiality cannot be contained within a single discipline.</p>

<p>Several presenters were particularly close to my own interests: <strong>Wen-shing Chou</strong> on Buddhist art in China and Inner Asia, <strong>Seunghye Lee</strong> on Chinese and Korean Buddhist art and image consecration, <strong>Maya Stiller</strong> on Korean Buddhist visual culture, and <strong>Trent Walker</strong> on textual and musical practices in Southeast Asian Buddhism. Bringing China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, and Southeast Asia into the same conversation made comparison unusually productive.</p>

<figure class="fieldwork-figure-wide"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-05.webp" alt="Conference room at Princeton" loading="lazy"><figcaption>For several days, the conference room became a collective laboratory for thinking about ritual and materiality.</figcaption></figure>

<h2>The organizers</h2>
<p>The conference was co-organized by <strong>Stephen F. Teiser</strong>, D. T. Suzuki Professor in Buddhist Studies and Professor of Religion at Princeton, and <strong>Shih-shan Susan Huang</strong> of Rice University. Teiser’s research on Chinese Buddhism, ritual, rebirth imagery, and manuscript traditions has reshaped the study of medieval Chinese Buddhism. Huang, an art historian trained at Yale, works on Daoist visual culture, Buddhist books and printing, and transnational circulation of images and texts. Their collaboration captured the central ambition of the meeting: to place religious history and visual culture in sustained dialogue.</p>

<p>Graduate co-convenors <strong>Kentaro Ide</strong> and <strong>Sinae Kim</strong>, together with conference coordinator <strong>Junbin Tan</strong>, also played a central role. The meeting was made possible by the <strong>Glorisun Global Buddhist Network</strong> and supported by Princeton units including the Tang Center for East Asian Art, Humanities Council, East Asian Studies Program, Center for Culture, Society &amp; Religion, and Department of Religion.</p>

<div class="figure-pair"><figure class="figure-item"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-07.webp" alt="Group at Princeton Department of East Asian Studies" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Conversations continued beyond the formal sessions within Princeton’s East Asian Studies community.</figcaption></figure><figure class="figure-item"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-06.webp" alt="Conference group dinner in Princeton" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The shared dinner was another important space for informal exchange among doctoral students and senior scholars.</figcaption></figure></div>

<h2>Why the experience mattered</h2>
<p>Being one of the twenty selected doctoral students mattered less as an abstract distinction than as access to an unusually concentrated scholarly environment. For several days I could speak directly with researchers whose work intersected with my questions about Korea, artistic patronage, consecration rituals, transregional circulation, and the material uses of Buddhist images. Conversations with doctoral students working on very different regions also forced me to explain my own project differently and to identify what could genuinely be compared across cultural areas.</p>

<figure class="fieldwork-figure-wide"><img src="/assets/images/princeton-09.webp" alt="Gothic architecture at Princeton University" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Between sessions, the campus continually recalled the historical scale of the institution hosting the meeting.</figcaption></figure>

<p>What I remember most is that the scholarly discussion never really stopped at the conference-room door. It continued in corridors, over meals, and while crossing the campus. For a young researcher working on the visual and material cultures of Buddhism in East Asia, the week was an important stage in situating my own research within an international network and in seeing more clearly how art history changes when objects are studied together with gestures, bodies, texts, and ritual practices.</p>
